items.stem: Which of the following best describes "global well-being"?
options: Repeated bullying through digital technologies, such as threatening messages, exclusion or sharing humiliating content
Patterns of smartphone use that interfere with sleep, relationships, work or well-being
The use of digital technologies – telemedicine, apps, wearables, health records and AI – to improve health and health care
The physical, mental and social health and quality of life of people around the world, which digital technologies can improve or harm
items.answer: The physical, mental and social health and quality of life of people around the world, which digital technologies can improve or harm
items.markingKey: D. "global well-being" is the physical, mental and social health and quality of life of people around the world, which digital technologies can improve or harm.

items.stem: Explain why online harms are a global rather than national challenge.
items.answer: Platforms operate across borders, harmful content and abusers can be anywhere, and national laws reach only part of the problem, so cooperation and global platform standards are needed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Platforms operate across borders, harmful content and abusers can be anywhere, and national laws reach only part of the problem, so cooperation and global platform standards are needed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Online harms only affect children." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Adults also face harassment, scams, misinformation and image-based abuse; women journalists and public figures are frequent targets.
items.markingKey: Adults also face harassment, scams, misinformation and image-based abuse; women journalists and public figures are frequent targets. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"It's time to require a surgeon general's warning label on social media platforms."
— Vivek Murthy, US Surgeon General, New York Times op-ed, June 2024

Explain the perspective expressed in the source.
items.answer: It treats social media as a public-health risk comparable to tobacco, arguing that users and parents need warnings about potential harm to young people's mental health.
items.markingKey: It treats social media as a public-health risk comparable to tobacco, arguing that users and parents need warnings about potential harm to young people's mental health. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A survey of 800 teenagers in Brazil found that 52% of 14–16-year-olds and 27% of 11–13-year-olds report losing sleep because of late-night phone use. Calculate the difference in percentage points and how many times more likely 14–16-year-olds were to report this. Explain why this survey does not prove that social media causes the harm.
items.answer: 25 percentage points; 1.9 times; it shows correlation; self-reported data; other factors (e.g. existing anxiety) may cause both; direction of causation unclear
items.markingKey: 52 − 27 = 25 pp [A1]; 52 ÷ 27 = 1.9 [M1 A1]. Correlation vs causation; self-report; confounders/reverse causation [R1 R1].

items.stem: Briefly describe mHealth messaging in Africa and explain what it reveals about digital technology improving well-being.
items.answer: Programmes such as MomConnect in South Africa (launched 2014) send pregnant women health information by SMS and WhatsApp, reaching millions of users. Low-cost mobile messaging extended maternal health information at scale, showing positive impacts on well-being.
items.markingKey: Context (Programmes such as MomConnect in South Africa (launched 2014) send pregnant women health information by SMS and WhatsApp, reaching millions of users.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: low-cost mobile messaging extended maternal health information at scale, showing positive impacts on well-being. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to digital technology improving well-being.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Social media does more harm than good to young people's well-being."
items.answer: Social media harms some young people significantly, especially vulnerable users, but benefits others; design and use matter more than presence or absence.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: links to anxiety, body image issues, sleep loss (Facebook Files); harmful content and cyberbullying (Molly Russell). Arguments against: support communities, creativity and connection; research shows small average effects and wide variation; benefits for marginalised youth (LGBTQ+). Supported judgement: Social media harms some young people significantly, especially vulnerable users, but benefits others; design and use matter more than presence or absence.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that digital technologies have improved global health more than they have harmed it.
items.answer: Overall health benefits are substantial, but harms to mental health and information quality require interventions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: telemedicine, mHealth and disease surveillance; information access. Arguments against: misinformation (COVID infodemic); mental-health and sedentary-lifestyle concerns; unequal access. Supported judgement: Overall health benefits are substantial, but harms to mental health and information quality require interventions. items.stem: Briefly explain why digital technologies can improve global well-being.
items.answer: They extend health information and services (telemedicine, mobile health messaging), connect isolated people, support mental-health apps and crisis lines, and enable early warning in emergencies.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They extend health information and services (telemedicine, mobile health messaging), connect isolated people, support mental-health apps and crisis lines, and enable early warning in emergencies. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the impact of social media on teenagers' mental health is difficult to establish.
items.answer: Studies are mostly correlational and self-reported; effects vary by individual, platform and type of use; heavy use may be a symptom as well as a cause; and researchers have limited access to platform data.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Studies are mostly correlational and self-reported; effects vary by individual, platform and type of use; heavy use may be a symptom as well as a cause; and researchers have limited access to platform data. items.answer: Online harms occur through digital platforms and can be persistent, anonymous, and spread rapidly to large audiences (e.g. cyberbullying 24/7); offline harms occur in physical settings and are usually more limited in reach and visibility.
items.markingKey: Online harms occur through digital platforms and can be persistent, anonymous, and spread rapidly to large audiences (e.g. cyberbullying 24/7); offline harms occur in physical settings and are usually more limited in reach and visibility. items.answer: Teen Accounts

items.stem: Explain why design changes can be more effective than education alone in protecting users.
items.answer: Defaults shape behaviour for millions automatically (most users never change settings), whereas education depends on individuals remembering and choosing to act.

items.stem: A student claims: "Banning children from social media will solve online harms." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Bans can be bypassed (false ages, VPNs), may push children to less regulated spaces, cut off benefits, and do not address harms to adults or platform design.
items.markingKey: Bans can be bypassed (false ages, VPNs), may push children to less regulated spaces, cut off benefits, and do not address harms to adults or platform design. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Australia's social-media minimum age law (2024) as an example, explain a ban as an intervention.
items.answer: Australia legislated that platforms must take reasonable steps to prevent under-16s having accounts, with fines up to A$49.5 million; it took effect in December 2025. It is one of the strictest interventions globally, testing whether age-based bans can be enforced and whether they improve well-being.
items.markingKey: Context (Australia legislated that platforms must take reasonable steps to prevent under-16s having accounts, with fines up to A$49.5 million; it took effect in December 2025.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. "Kids will find a way around it, and we'll push them into darker corners of the internet."
— Digital-rights advocate commenting on Australia's under-16 social-media law, 2024

Explain one possible unintended consequence of the intervention suggested by the source.
items.answer: Children may lie about their age or use unregulated platforms, where harms may be greater and there are fewer protections.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Age Appropriate Design Code"?

A deliberate action by a government, organisation or community to address a challenge, such as a law, design change or education programme
An outcome of an intervention that was not planned or expected, which may be positive or negative
The UK code (2021) requiring online services likely to be used by children to apply 15 standards, such as high privacy by default
items.answer: The UK code (2021) requiring online services likely to be used by children to apply 15 standards, such as high privacy by default

items.stem: Distinguish between a ban and a duty of care.
items.answer: A ban prohibits an activity outright (e.g. under-16s on social media in Australia); a duty of care requires platforms to assess and reduce risks while still allowing use.
items.markingKey: A ban prohibits an activity outright (e.g. under-16s on social media in Australia); a duty of care requires platforms to assess and reduce risks while still allowing use. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using the UK Online Safety Act 2023 as an example, explain a regulatory intervention for well-being.
items.answer: The Act requires platforms to assess and reduce risks of illegal content and protect children from harmful content, enforced by Ofcom with fines up to 10% of global turnover; children's codes applied from 2025. It creates legal duties of care, but critics raise concerns about privacy (encryption) and over-removal.
items.markingKey: Context (The Act requires platforms to assess and reduce risks of illegal content and protect children from harmful content, enforced by Ofcom with fines up to 10% of global turnover; children's codes applied from 2025.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: "Raising the minimum age for social media will improve young people's well-being." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Age limits may help some young people, but effectiveness depends on enforcement and on improving platform design for all users.

items.stem: Which criterion asks whether an intervention benefits different groups fairly?
items.answer: Equity
items.markingKey: Equity. Equity considers distribution of benefits and burdens.

items.stem: A student claims: "An intervention that achieves its main goal is a success." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It may still have serious unintended consequences or unfair impacts on some stakeholders, and may be too costly or infringe rights; evaluation must consider all of these.
items.markingKey: It may still have serious unintended consequences or unfair impacts on some stakeholders, and may be too costly or infringe rights; evaluation must consider all of these. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between effectiveness and efficiency.
items.answer: Effectiveness is whether an intervention achieves its goal; efficiency is whether it does so at reasonable cost relative to alternatives.
items.markingKey: Effectiveness is whether an intervention achieves its goal; efficiency is whether it does so at reasonable cost relative to alternatives. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
A government is choosing an intervention for reducing harm to teenagers on social media. Each option is scored 1–5 (5 = best) on impact on rights (weight 0.6), feasibility (weight 0.2) and cost (weight 0.2).
age-verification law: impact on rights 1, feasibility 4, cost 5
default "teen accounts" with limits: impact on rights 5, feasibility 4, cost 2
school digital-wellbeing lessons: impact on rights 1, feasibility 1, cost 2
Calculate the weighted score of each option and identify which should be recommended.
items.answer: age-verification law 2.4; default "teen accounts" with limits 4.2; school digital-wellbeing lessons 1.2; recommend default "teen accounts" with limits
items.markingKey: age-verification law: 0.6×1 + 0.2×4 + 0.2×5 = 2.4; default "teen accounts" with limits: 0.6×5 + 0.2×4 + 0.2×2 = 4.2; school digital-wellbeing lessons: 0.6×1 + 0.2×1 + 0.2×2 = 1.2 [M1 A1 A1]; highest = default "teen accounts" with limits [A1].

items.stem: Outline one way in which age verification for adult websites in parts of the US shows unintended consequences.
items.answer: Several US states required age verification for adult sites from 2023; some major sites withdrew from those states and VPN searches rose. Users shifted to VPNs and less regulated sites, showing how interventions can displace rather than reduce harm.
items.markingKey: Context (Several US states required age verification for adult sites from 2023; some major sites withdrew from those states and VPN searches rose.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: users shifted to VPNs and less regulated sites, showing how interventions can displace rather than reduce harm. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to unintended consequences.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The most important criterion for evaluating a digital intervention is its effectiveness."
items.answer: Effectiveness is central, but must be weighed against rights, equity and side effects to judge whether an intervention is justified.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: an ineffective intervention wastes resources; effectiveness is the purpose of intervening. Arguments against: rights, equity and unintended consequences matter; a highly effective intervention can be disproportionate (e.g. shutdowns); feasibility and cost determine whether it can be sustained. Supported judgement: Effectiveness is central, but must be weighed against rights, equity and side effects to judge whether an intervention is justified.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "stakeholder"?

Any individual, group or organisation affected by or able to influence an intervention
Building protections into products from the start, such as private-by-default accounts for children
A UK law giving Ofcom powers to require platforms to protect users, especially children, from illegal and harmful content

items.markingKey: B. "stakeholder" is any individual, group or organisation affected by or able to influence an intervention.

items.stem: Briefly explain why unintended consequences should be considered when evaluating interventions.
items.answer: Interventions change behaviour in complex systems; ignoring side effects (displacement, privacy loss, chilling effects) can make an intervention harmful overall even if it meets its main goal.

labels on AI-generated content: cost 2, impact on rights 3, effectiveness 5

items.stem: In 2022, a UK coroner concluded that online content contributed "in a more than minimal way" to the death of which teenager?
items.answer: Molly Russell
items.markingKey: D. The inquest examined Instagram and Pinterest content she had viewed.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Building protections into products from the start, such as private-by-default accounts for children"?
items.answer: safety by design

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "How practical an intervention is to implement given costs, technology, politics and time"?
items.answer: feasibility

items.stem: Distinguish between digital well-being risks and digital health opportunities.
items.answer: Opportunities include better access to care, monitoring and information; risks include addiction, misinformation, privacy breaches and exposure to harmful content.
items.markingKey: Opportunities include better access to care, monitoring and information; risks include addiction, misinformation, privacy breaches and exposure to harmful content. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Diego writes: "Digital well-being features are designed mainly to help users." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They can help, but companies also introduce them in response to regulatory and public pressure; they are usually optional and may be less prominent than engagement features.
items.markingKey: They can help, but companies also introduce them in response to regulatory and public pressure; they are usually optional and may be less prominent than engagement features. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between efficiency and effectiveness.
items.answer: Effectiveness is whether an intervention achieves its goal; efficiency is whether it does so at reasonable cost relative to alternatives.
items.markingKey: Effectiveness is whether an intervention achieves its goal; efficiency is whether it does so at reasonable cost relative to alternatives. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Screen time is the main cause of the teenage mental-health crisis." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Researchers disagree: some (e.g. Jonathan Haidt) argue phones and social media are a major cause, while others (e.g. Candice Odgers, Amy Orben) find small average effects and point to other factors; type of use matters more than total time.

items.stem: Explain why evidence of effectiveness is often limited for digital interventions.
items.answer: Many are new, platforms control the data, outcomes such as well-being are hard to measure, and it is difficult to isolate the effect of one intervention from other changes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Many are new, platforms control the data, outcomes such as well-being are hard to measure, and it is difficult to isolate the effect of one intervention from other changes. items.stem: Using the Facebook Files (2021) as an example, explain corporate knowledge of digital harms.
items.answer: Frances Haugen leaked internal research showing Meta knew Instagram could worsen body image and anxiety for some teenage girls. Evidence that a company knew of harms intensified calls for duties of care and transparency.

items.stem: Using China's limits on minors' online gaming (2021) as an example, explain state intervention in digital well-being.
items.answer: Regulators limited under-18s to one hour of online gaming on Fridays, weekends and holidays, enforced by real-name verification. Strict limits reduced gaming time for many minors, but relied on identity verification and state control that raise privacy concerns.
items.markingKey: Context (Regulators limited under-18s to one hour of online gaming on Fridays, weekends and holidays, enforced by real-name verification.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem:
A government is choosing an intervention for closing the rural connectivity gap. Each option is scored 1–5 (5 = best) on equity (weight 0.5), effectiveness (weight 0.3) and impact on rights (weight 0.2).
satellite broadband vouchers: equity 4, effectiveness 2, impact on rights 1
community Wi-Fi hubs: equity 2, effectiveness 4, impact on rights 5
subsidised mobile data plans: equity 2, effectiveness 5, impact on rights 4
Calculate the weighted score of each option and identify which should be recommended.
items.answer: satellite broadband vouchers 2.8; community Wi-Fi hubs 3.2; subsidised mobile data plans 3.3; recommend subsidised mobile data plans
items.markingKey: satellite broadband vouchers: 0.5×4 + 0.3×2 + 0.2×1 = 2.8; community Wi-Fi hubs: 0.5×2 + 0.3×4 + 0.2×5 = 3.2; subsidised mobile data plans: 0.5×2 + 0.3×5 + 0.2×4 = 3.3 [M1 A1 A1]; highest = subsidised mobile data plans [A1].

items.stem: A survey of 1,500 teenagers in Australia found that 52% of girls and 45% of boys have experienced online bullying in the past year. Calculate the difference in percentage points and how many times more likely girls were to report this. Explain why this survey does not prove that social media causes the harm.
items.answer: 7 percentage points; 1.2 times; it shows correlation; self-reported data; other factors (e.g. existing anxiety) may cause both; direction of causation unclear
items.markingKey: 52 − 45 = 7 pp [A1]; 52 ÷ 45 = 1.2 [M1 A1]. Correlation vs causation; self-report; confounders/reverse causation [R1 R1].

items.stem: Outline one way in which the UK Online Safety Act 2023 shows a regulatory intervention for well-being.
items.answer: The Act requires platforms to assess and reduce risks of illegal content and protect children from harmful content, enforced by Ofcom with fines up to 10% of global turnover; children's codes applied from 2025. It creates legal duties of care, but critics raise concerns about privacy (encryption) and over-removal.
items.markingKey: Context (The Act requires platforms to assess and reduce risks of illegal content and protect children from harmful content, enforced by Ofcom with fines up to 10% of global turnover; children's codes applied from 2025.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Read the source below.

"Hiding like counts made some people feel better, but others found it annoying. So we're giving people the choice."
— Paraphrase of Instagram's announcement, May 2021

items.answer: Its effects were mixed across users – beneficial for some, unwelcome for others – so Instagram made it optional rather than universal.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that the most important criterion for evaluating a digital intervention is its effectiveness.
items.answer: Effectiveness is central, but must be weighed against rights, equity and side effects to judge whether an intervention is justified.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: an ineffective intervention wastes resources; effectiveness is the purpose of intervening. Arguments against: rights, equity and unintended consequences matter; a highly effective intervention can be disproportionate (e.g. shutdowns); feasibility and cost determine whether it can be sustained. Supported judgement: Effectiveness is central, but must be weighed against rights, equity and side effects to judge whether an intervention is justified. items.stem: "Social media does more harm than good to young people's well-being." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Social media harms some young people significantly, especially vulnerable users, but benefits others; design and use matter more than presence or absence.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that raising the minimum age for social media will improve young people's well-being.
items.answer: Age limits may help some young people, but effectiveness depends on enforcement and on improving platform design for all users.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: reduces exposure to harmful content and comparison; gives parents support to set limits. Arguments against: easy to bypass; age verification raises privacy issues; loss of social connection and support; evidence of causal benefit is limited. Supported judgement: Age limits may help some young people, but effectiveness depends on enforcement and on improving platform design for all users.
